# Media and the Browser

A player turns received objects into sound and pictures. MOQT delivers the objects; the media format and player tell the browser how to interpret, decode, and present them.

We will follow that path in order: read the media description, find a decodable starting point, submit encoded data to a decoder, and schedule the result for playback. The final section covers browser permissions and resource cleanup. Our examples use the moq.dev **hang** media layer and the browser's **WebCodecs** API, both of which we will introduce below.

## How does the player interpret a track? {#discovering-the-media}

The lecture offers an audio track and two video tracks, one at a lower resolution for slower connections. Track names let the player request them, but names alone do not explain how to use their bytes. The player also needs the codec, decoder configuration, and timing information. A **codec** defines how pictures or sound are encoded and decoded. A **container** packages the encoded data with information needed to interpret it, such as timestamps.

MOQT carries application payloads without choosing their media format. Our example uses **hang**, the media layer in the moq.dev stack. Its `catalog.json` track describes the available renditions and their decoder configuration. A rendition is an alternative encoding of the content, such as the lecture's lower-resolution picture. See the [hang catalog and container documentation](https://doc.moq.dev/concept/hang).

Suppose the selected video rendition contains H.264 pictures at 1280 × 720 pixels. Its codec identifier tells the player which decoder it needs. Its codec configuration supplies any required setup, either as initialization data or in-band as the format permits, and its container field tells the player how to find the encoded chunks and their timestamps. With this information, the player can check support on the student's device and subscribe to a suitable track.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    accTitle: From a lecture catalog to a displayed picture
    accDescr: The player reads the catalog, selects a supported rendition, receives its media objects, parses encoded chunks and timestamps, decodes pictures, then schedules and displays them.
    A[Read the media catalog] --> B[Choose a supported rendition]
    B --> C[Subscribe and receive objects]
    C --> D[Parse chunks and timestamps]
    D --> E[Decode pictures]
    E --> F[Schedule and display]
    A -. Decoder configuration .-> E
    D -. Media timestamps .-> F
```

The catalog remains useful after playback starts. The lecturer might add screen sharing, or a rendition might temporarily become unavailable. The player needs to respond to those updates instead of treating the initial list as permanent.

### What does container parsing actually do?

Knowing the codec is not enough to pass a whole received payload to a decoder. In hang's `legacy` container, a frame begins with a variable-length timestamp in microseconds, followed by encoded media. The player reads that timestamp, removes the container header, and supplies the encoded portion to the decoder with the appropriate timing information. Other containers have different layouts. Use the catalog's container declaration, not a guess based on the codec. See the [hang container formats](https://doc.moq.dev/concept/hang#containers).

For example, mistaking timestamp bytes for H.264 data can produce a decoder failure even when delivery was perfect. This is why parsing has its own step in the diagram.

### Four things that are easy to confuse

| Term | What it describes | In the lecture |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Codec | How media is compressed and reconstructed | H.264 video |
| Rendition | One encoding offered to the viewer | A 720p version of the lecturer’s camera |
| MoQ object | An addressed unit delivered by the transport | A payload identified by its track, group, and object IDs |
| Decoded frame | A picture the decoder has reconstructed | A `VideoFrame` the player can render |

An **encoded chunk** is a unit of compressed media submitted to a decoder. The media format defines how these chunks fit into objects. MOQT itself does not require one object to equal one video frame. Keeping that boundary clear helps locate failures: receiving an object proves delivery, while displaying a picture also requires parsing, decoding, and scheduling.

## Where can decoding begin? {#starting-with-a-decodable-picture}

Video compression often describes how one picture differs from earlier pictures. Such a predicted frame is useful only when the decoder has the reference pictures it needs. A **keyframe** supplies a fresh decoding starting point in the video model we are using.

This explains the group boundaries from the object-model chapter. The publisher starts a video group with a keyframe, then places dependent frames after it. Our late-arriving student can retrieve the beginning of the current group or wait for the next group. Receiving only the middle of a group may leave the decoder without its references, even though every requested byte arrived correctly.

The encoder and packager must agree on those boundaries. Cutting a stream every second does not itself create independent video sequences. The media format also has to supply the decoder configuration needed at the join point.

The same issue appears when the student switches to higher resolution. The new rendition has its own decoder state. The player changes configuration as needed and starts at a valid decoding point; it cannot simply feed an arbitrary high-resolution predicted frame into the old sequence.

## How does WebCodecs decode the media? {#decoding-in-the-browser}

WebCodecs gives JavaScript access to media encoders and decoders. For video, the player checks a configuration with `VideoDecoder.isConfigSupported()`, applies it with `configure()`, and submits encoded chunks with `decode()`. Support depends on the actual codec configuration and device, so the presence of the API alone is insufficient.

The decoder produces `VideoFrame` objects through an output callback. Those are decoded pictures ready for the next stage, rather than instructions to display immediately. The player owns the queues, presentation timing, and rendering. It also parses the incoming container before submitting chunks. These responsibilities explain why WebCodecs is a component of a player rather than a complete player. The [VideoDecoder interface](https://www.w3.org/TR/webcodecs/#videodecoder-interface) describes the API.

Each decoded frame holds resources. After rendering or discarding a frame, the player calls `VideoFrame.close()` when it no longer needs that frame. Waiting for garbage collection can retain scarce resources and stall decoding. Bounded queues are equally important: if rendering slows down, receiving more frames must not cause unlimited memory growth. See the [WebCodecs memory model](https://www.w3.org/TR/webcodecs/#raw-media-memory-model).

## When should a frame be presented? {#choosing-when-to-play}

Frames do not necessarily arrive at the spacing at which they were captured. Variable network delay produces **jitter**. If the player displayed pictures on arrival, that uneven timing would become visible movement on the screen.

Media timestamps preserve the intended spacing. Consider these illustrative values, in milliseconds. The media timeline and receiver clock have different origins. These teaching values use milliseconds; WebCodecs `VideoFrame.timestamp` uses [microseconds](https://www.w3.org/TR/webcodecs/#dom-videoframe-timestamp), so a player must convert units when mapping clocks.

| Frame | Media timestamp | Arrival on receiver clock | Planned display on receiver clock |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| A | 0 | 100 | 160 |
| B | 33 | 145 | 193 |
| C | 67 | 150 | 227 |

The player chooses receiver time 160 as the moment to display media time zero. It adds each subsequent media timestamp to that anchor. Although B and C arrive only five milliseconds apart, the player displays them 34 milliseconds apart, preserving the media timeline.

### Arrival time and presentation time

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    accTitle: Uneven arrivals become evenly scheduled presentation
    accDescr: Frame A arrives at receiver time 100 and is displayed at 160. B arrives at 145 and is displayed at 193. C arrives at 150 and is displayed at 227. Each frame waits until its scheduled display time.
    A["A arrives: 100 ms"] -->|"Wait 60 ms"| D["Display A: 160 ms"]
    B["B arrives: 145 ms"] -->|"Wait 48 ms"| E["Display B: 193 ms"]
    C["C arrives: 150 ms"] -->|"Wait 77 ms"| F["Display C: 227 ms"]
```

Each arrow follows one frame through the playback buffer. The diagram uses the table's receiver clock; arrow lengths are not a time scale.

The initial wait gives later frames some room to arrive. If B instead arrives at receiver time 205, it misses its planned time of 193. The player must then apply its late-frame policy, perhaps skipping the picture or moving playback later. That is the buffering tradeoff: waiting longer can absorb more variation, at the cost of a later picture.

### Keeping audio and video together

Audio follows the same presentation timeline. An audio sample and a picture intended for media time 67 ms can arrive separately; the player schedules them against a shared clock so the lecturer's voice stays aligned with their face. Over longer sessions it may also need to correct differences between clocks.

Group and object IDs locate content; the media timestamps tell the player when to present it. Neither this table nor those IDs measure capture-to-display latency by themselves. That measurement also requires a relationship between the source's capture clock and the receiver's clock.

## What else does a browser player need? {#completing-the-player}

A student pressing Play brings the rest of the browser into the picture. Playback may require a user action under autoplay policy. A publisher capturing a camera or microphone needs capture permission; publishing a supplied file does not require access to those devices. See the [media capture permission rules](https://www.w3.org/TR/mediacapture-streams/#dom-mediadevices-getusermedia). Devices can disappear, tabs can become hidden, and the page must release resources when the session ends.

The moq.dev project provides higher-level player and publisher packages that handle much of this integration. Using its existing player gives a first experiment a working path through capture, decoding, and presentation. The chapter's pipeline then provides a way to investigate a failure: determine whether the missing step is media discovery, a decodable starting point, decoding, or presentation.
